  • For Windows VMs, the Azure VM agent orchestrates with Windows Update. For Linux VMs, it integrates with the native package manager (apt, yum, zypper). Prerequisites include the Azure VM agent being healthy and outbound connectivity to update sources.
  • Coordinate patching with application availability. Use Azure Update Manager's pre and post scripts to drain load balancer connections before patching and re-enable them after, ensuring zero-downtime updates for multi-instance workloads.

questions.title: Storage Immutability Requirement
questions.scenario: Legal requires retention of certain blobs for 7 years with WORM semantics.

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: WORM means data cannot be altered or deleted once written. Which Azure Storage feature enforces that at the platform level?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Immutable blob storage policy (A) is correct because it enforces WORM semantics by preventing blob deletion and modification for a specified retention period. You can configure either a time-based retention policy (lock blobs for a set duration like 7 years) or a legal hold (lock indefinitely until the hold is removed). Option B (soft delete) allows recovery of deleted blobs but does not prevent deletion in the first place. Option C (lifecycle management) automates tiering and deletion, which is the opposite of WORM retention. Option D (versioning) preserves previous versions but does not prevent deletion of the blob itself. Only immutability policies provide the regulatory-grade WORM guarantees that legal and compliance teams require.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Time-based retention policies can be in unlocked state (allowing extensions) or locked state (irreversible, cannot be shortened or removed even by the storage account owner). For regulatory compliance like SEC 17a-4, the policy must be locked. Once locked, the storage account cannot be deleted until all retention periods expire.
  • Legal holds are separate from time-based policies and are tag-based. Multiple legal holds can be applied simultaneously (e.g., one per legal case). Blobs remain immutable until all legal hold tags are cleared. Legal holds do not have an expiration date.
  • Immutability policies interact with other storage features in important ways: lifecycle management delete actions will fail on immutable blobs, versioning creates immutable versions, and blob soft delete applies after the retention period expires. Plan these interactions carefully.
  • Azure immutable storage is compliant with SEC 17a-4(f), CFTC 1.31(c)-(d), and FINRA 4511. For healthcare (HIPAA) or other regulatory frameworks, verify the specific compliance certification in the Azure compliance documentation before committing to the architecture.

questions.title: Restore vs Recreate (Disaster Recovery Thinking)
questions.scenario: A VM is corrupted after a bad change. You have backups.
questions.questionText: What's the fastest likely recovery path?

choices.text: Restore from backup (or restore disks) and redeploy
Wait for the VM to self-heal

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: When a VM is corrupted and you have recent backups, the fastest path is to restore to a known good state rather than rebuilding from scratch or waiting.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Restoring from backup or restoring disks and redeploying (C) is the fastest recovery path because Azure Backup maintains application-consistent snapshots that can be restored to a known good point-in-time. You can either restore the full VM (creates a new VM from the backup) or restore just the disks and attach them to an existing or new VM. Option A (rebuild from scratch) requires reinstalling the OS, applications, and data, which takes significantly longer. Option B (Azure Support) adds wait time and is appropriate for platform issues, not customer-caused corruption. Option D (self-heal) is not how Azure VMs work when the OS or application is corrupted. The backup restore preserves all data and configuration up to the backup point.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Azure Backup offers multiple restore options: Create New VM (provisions a new VM from backup), Restore Disks (restores managed disks to a storage account or resource group for manual attachment), and Replace Existing (swaps the current VM disks with backup versions). Choose based on whether you need the original VM identity, IP, and configuration preserved.
  • If a security incident is suspected (malware, ransomware), restore into an isolated quarantine VNet first. Do not restore to the production network until the backup has been scanned and validated. This prevents re-infection from a compromised backup.
  • Restore time depends on the backup tier. Instant restore from the snapshot tier (retained 1-5 days) takes minutes because the data is already in managed disk snapshots. Vault-tier restores require data transfer from the vault and can take hours depending on VM size and disk count.
  • For critical workloads, test restore procedures regularly. A backup that has never been test-restored is an assumption, not a guarantee. Document the restore runbook including network configuration, DNS updates, and application startup verification steps.

questions.title: Diagnose Storage Access Denied
questions.scenario: An app gets "403 Forbidden" accessing a blob. It uses Entra ID auth.
questions.questionText: What are the top likely causes?

choices.text: Missing RBAC role, wrong scope, or token/audience mismatch

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: A 403 means authentication succeeded but authorization failed. What three areas should you check when an identity is recognized but still denied?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Missing RBAC role, wrong scope, or token/audience mismatch (D) covers the most common causes of 403 errors with Entra ID authentication. The app identity might lack a data-plane role (e.g., Storage Blob Data Reader), or the role might be assigned at the wrong scope (subscription level instead of storage account or container). The token audience might be incorrect (requesting a token for https://management.azure.com instead of https://storage.azure.com). Option A (blob does not exist) returns 404, not 403. Option B (global outage) would affect all customers and be visible on the Azure status page. Option C (deleted account) returns DNS resolution failure or 404, not 403. Always check the exact error response body, which usually contains the specific authorization failure reason.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• The most subtle cause is the control-plane vs data-plane role confusion. Storage Account Contributor (control-plane) manages the storage account settings but grants zero data access. Storage Blob Data Contributor (data-plane) grants blob read/write/delete. This is the number one 403 cause for teams new to Entra ID storage authentication.
  • Network restrictions can also cause 403 errors. If the storage account firewall blocks the client IP or VNet, the request is denied at the network layer before RBAC is even evaluated. Check the storage account networking tab for allowed networks, especially if using private endpoints.
  • Token audience mismatch occurs when the application requests an OAuth token for the wrong resource. For Azure Storage, the token must be requested for the resource https://storage.azure.com/. Using the wrong audience (e.g., the Key Vault or Graph API audience) results in a valid token that Storage rejects.
  • RBAC role propagation can take up to 10 minutes after assignment. If you just assigned a role and immediately tested, the 403 may be a timing issue. Wait 10 minutes and retry before investigating further. Check effective access in the portal under the storage account IAM blade.

questions.title: "I Can Ping But Not Connect"
questions.scenario: Two VMs in same VNet can ping but cannot connect on TCP/1433.
questions.questionText: What's the most likely Azure control?

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Ping works but a specific TCP port does not. What does that tell you about where the block is — network reachability or port-level filtering?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: NSG rules blocking TCP/1433 (C) is the most likely cause. ICMP (ping) and TCP are different protocols evaluated independently by NSG rules. A successful ping means the VMs have IP connectivity and NSG allows ICMP, but the NSG may have no rule allowing TCP/1433 (SQL Server default port), or a deny rule may be blocking it. Option A (VNet peering) is irrelevant since the VMs are in the same VNet and ping works. Option B (storage account firewall) has nothing to do with VM-to-VM connectivity. Option D (DNS failure) would prevent ping by hostname, but the scenario implies connectivity exists since ping succeeds. Always check effective security rules for both the source and destination NICs/subnets when troubleshooting port-specific failures.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• NSGs evaluate rules per protocol and port. Default NSG rules allow all intra-VNet traffic (AllowVnetInBound, priority 65000), but any custom deny rule with a lower priority number will override this default. A rule like "Deny TCP Any 1433" at priority 100 blocks SQL while allowing ICMP ping.
  • Use the Effective Security Rules view on the destination VM NIC to see the merged rule set from both subnet and NIC NSGs. This shows exactly which rules apply and in what priority order, which is faster than manually reading multiple NSG configurations.
  • If NSG rules look correct, also check the OS-level firewall on the destination VM. Windows Firewall and Linux iptables/firewalld can independently block ports. SQL Server installations on Windows sometimes do not open port 1433 in Windows Firewall by default.
  • Network Watcher IP Flow Verify is the definitive tool for this scenario. Specify the source VM, destination VM IP, TCP protocol, and port 1433. It tells you whether the packet is allowed or denied and by which specific NSG rule, eliminating guesswork.

questions.title: Private Endpoint vs Service Endpoint
questions.scenario: You need private connectivity to a PaaS service and want the service to have a private IP in your VNet.

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Only one of these options creates an actual network interface with a private IP address inside your VNet that maps to the PaaS resource.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Private Endpoint (C) is correct because it creates a network interface in your VNet subnet with a private IP address that maps to a specific PaaS resource instance. Traffic flows over the private IP without traversing the public internet. Option A (Service Endpoint) optimizes the routing path to keep traffic on the Microsoft backbone, but the PaaS service retains its public IP and no private IP is created in your VNet. Option B (VPN Gateway) connects on-premises to Azure, not VNets to PaaS services. Option D (ExpressRoute) provides private on-premises connectivity but does not assign PaaS resources a VNet IP. The requirement for "a private IP in your VNet" is the decisive factor pointing to Private Endpoint.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Private Endpoints require DNS alignment. The PaaS service FQDN (e.g., mydb.database.windows.net) must resolve to the private IP. This is typically achieved with an Azure Private DNS zone (e.g., privatelink.database.windows.net) linked to the VNet. Without correct DNS, clients connect to the public endpoint despite the Private Endpoint existing.
  • Service Endpoints are simpler and free (no per-hour charge) but do not meet "no public endpoint" requirements. The PaaS service still has a public FQDN and IP, with firewall rules restricting access to specific VNet subnets. Traffic stays on the backbone but is not truly private from a network architecture perspective.
  • Private Endpoints support cross-region access: a VNet in East US can have a Private Endpoint connected to a storage account in West Europe. This is useful for centralized data services accessed from multiple regions.
  • Each Private Endpoint consumes an IP address from the subnet. Plan subnet sizing accordingly, especially if you have many PaaS resources that each need a Private Endpoint. A /28 subnet provides 11 usable IPs (16 minus 5 Azure-reserved), enough for 11 Private Endpoints.

questions.title: Log Analytics Workspace Access
questions.scenario: A user can view VM resources but cannot query logs in Log Analytics.
questions.questionText: Why, and what do you change?

choices.text: The user needs Global Administrator role
Workspace permissions are separate; grant workspace access

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: The user can see VMs but cannot query their logs. Are resource permissions and log query permissions governed by the same RBAC assignment?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Workspace permissions are separate and must be explicitly granted (A). A user with Reader on a VM can see the VM resource in the portal but cannot query its logs in Log Analytics because the workspace has its own RBAC model. You need to assign a workspace-level role like Log Analytics Reader or Monitoring Reader on the Log Analytics workspace itself. Option B (Global Administrator) is massively over-privileged for reading logs. Option C is incorrect because Azure Monitor cannot be globally disabled. Option D is unlikely since the scenario implies logs exist but are inaccessible. The separation of resource RBAC and workspace RBAC is a common source of confusion for teams new to Azure monitoring.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Log Analytics supports two access control modes: workspace-context (permissions on the workspace grant access to all data in it) and resource-context (permissions on a resource grant access to that resource's logs in any workspace). The access mode is set on the workspace and affects how authorization is evaluated.
  • In resource-context mode, a user with Reader on a VM can query that VM's logs even without explicit workspace permissions. This is useful for large organizations where workspace admins should not have to manage per-user access. Check the workspace Access Control Mode setting in Properties.
  • Central Log Analytics workspaces often reside in a shared platform subscription, separate from the application subscriptions. Users need permissions at the workspace scope, which is in a different subscription than their application resources. Cross-subscription RBAC assignment is required.
  • For fine-grained access, use table-level RBAC to restrict users to specific log tables within the workspace (e.g., allow access to SecurityEvent but not ContainerLog). This is useful for compliance scenarios where different teams should only see specific data categories.

questions.title: Diagnostic Settings Coverage Gap
questions.scenario: You have a Log Analytics workspace but see no NSG flow logs or storage logs.

choices.text: Diagnostic settings not enabled on resources
The subscription is in a different region

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: You have a workspace but no data is arriving. Does Azure automatically send resource logs somewhere, or must you explicitly enable collection per resource?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Diagnostic settings not enabled on resources (A) is the most likely cause. Azure does not automatically send resource logs to any destination. You must create diagnostic settings on each resource (NSG, storage account, etc.) specifying which log categories to collect and where to send them (Log Analytics workspace, storage account, or Event Hub). Option B is irrelevant because diagnostic settings work cross-region. Option C is incorrect because Azure Monitor cannot be disabled globally. Option D (workspace full) is unlikely since Log Analytics workspaces have configurable daily caps but are not fixed-size. The most common monitoring gap is simply forgetting to enable diagnostic settings on newly deployed resources.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Use Azure Policy with the "Deploy diagnostic settings" effect (deployIfNotExists) to automatically configure diagnostic settings on resources as they are created. This eliminates the gap where new resources are deployed without monitoring. Apply the policy at the management group level for comprehensive coverage.
  • NSG flow logs have their own configuration separate from standard diagnostic settings. Flow logs are configured through Network Watcher and require a storage account as a destination. Optionally, Traffic Analytics can process flow logs and send summarized data to Log Analytics for visualization.
  • Each resource type has different available log categories. For example, a storage account has StorageRead, StorageWrite, and StorageDelete categories. Not all categories may be needed; select only those relevant to your monitoring requirements to control ingestion costs.
  • Diagnostic settings support three destinations: Log Analytics workspace (for querying and alerting), storage account (for long-term archival), and Event Hub (for streaming to external SIEM systems). You can configure multiple diagnostic settings on the same resource to send different log categories to different destinations.

questions.title: "I Need to See Who Changed This"
questions.scenario: You must identify who modified an NSG rule yesterday.

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: All Azure Resource Manager write operations, including who performed them and when, are recorded in a subscription-level audit log.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: The Activity Log (D) is where you look because it records all control-plane (ARM) operations for the subscription, including who modified the NSG rule, what was changed, when the change occurred, and whether it succeeded or failed. The caller identity, timestamp, and operation details are all captured. Option A (Azure Advisor) provides optimization recommendations, not audit trails. Option B (Resource Health) tracks resource availability status, not configuration changes. Option C (Cost Management) tracks spending, not administrative actions. For the NSG modification, filter the Activity Log by resource type (Network Security Groups), operation (Write), and time range (yesterday) to find the specific change event.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Activity Log entries are retained for 90 days in the portal by default. For longer retention or advanced querying, create a diagnostic setting to export the Activity Log to a Log Analytics workspace. This enables KQL queries like "who made the most NSG changes in the last 30 days" and alerting on suspicious patterns.
  • The Activity Log captures the Caller identity (UPN or service principal), the operation name (e.g., Microsoft.Network/networkSecurityGroups/securityRules/write), the result status (Succeeded, Failed), and the resource ID. However, it does not capture the before and after values of the changed properties.
  • To see what specifically changed in the NSG rule (the old value versus the new value), use Azure Resource Graph or check the Change Analysis feature in Azure Monitor. Change Analysis tracks property-level diffs and can show exactly which rule properties were modified.
  • In multi-subscription environments, each subscription has its own Activity Log. If you need a unified audit view, route all subscriptions' Activity Logs to a single Log Analytics workspace using per-subscription diagnostic settings.

questions.title: Resource Move: RG vs Subscription
questions.scenario: You must move a set of resources to a new subscription for billing separation.
questions.questionText: What are the two key prechecks?

choices.text: Check if resources are running and stop them
Delete the resources and recreate them
Validate move support and ensure dependencies/permissions across scopes

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Not all resource types can be moved, and a cross-subscription move spans two security boundaries. What two things must you verify before attempting it?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Validating move support and ensuring dependencies/permissions across scopes (C) is correct. The two critical prechecks are: (1) confirm each resource type supports cross-subscription move using the Azure documentation move support matrix, since some resources cannot be moved at all; (2) verify you have required permissions in both the source and destination subscriptions (typically Contributor on both, plus specific permissions for resource types that require them). Option A (stop resources) is unnecessary for most resource moves. Option B (delete and recreate) loses resource IDs, configurations, and data. Option D (contact Support) is unnecessary for standard moves. Additionally, use the Move Validation API to pre-check before executing the actual move.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Resource move support varies significantly by resource type. VMs, storage accounts, and VNets generally support cross-subscription moves, but some resources (classic resources, certain marketplace offerings) do not. Always check the official "Move operation support for resources" documentation before planning a move.
  • Dependent resources must be moved together or decoupled first. For example, a VM with managed disks, NICs, and a public IP must have all these resources moved in the same operation. If any dependency cannot be moved, the entire move fails validation.
  • RBAC role assignments are not moved with resources. After moving resources to a new subscription, re-create any role assignments that were specific to the old subscription scope. Managed identity associations may also need to be re-validated.
  • Azure Policy in the destination subscription can reject moved resources if they violate compliance rules (e.g., wrong tags, disallowed SKUs, missing configurations). Pre-check the destination subscription policies and remediate any expected compliance gaps before initiating the move.

questions.title: "Policy vs Lock" for Deletion Prevention
questions.scenario: You need to prevent accidental deletion of a resource group, but admins still must be able to deploy within it.

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: The requirement is narrow: block deletion but allow deployments. Which protection mechanism draws exactly that line?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: A CanNotDelete lock on the resource group (C) is the simplest control because it blocks deletion of the RG and its resources while allowing all other operations (create, update, read). Admins can continue deploying new resources and modifying existing ones normally. Option A (Policy with deny delete) is more complex to implement and maintain for this purpose and is better suited for broad governance rules. Option B (remove Contributor) prevents deployments, violating the requirement that admins must still deploy within the RG. Option D (move to a protected subscription) is excessive overhead for a single RG protection need. The CanNotDelete lock is a one-click setting that can be applied in seconds through the portal, CLI, or ARM template.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• CanNotDelete locks block delete operations but allow all modifications. ReadOnly locks block both deletions and modifications, which would prevent deployments. For this scenario, CanNotDelete is clearly the right choice. A ReadOnly lock would break the "admins must be able to deploy" requirement.
  • Locks are inherited by child resources. A CanNotDelete lock on the RG means no resource within it can be deleted either. This can interfere with IaC tools that use delete-and-recreate strategies for updates. If using Terraform or ARM templates with replace behavior, incorporate lock removal and reapplication into the deployment pipeline.
  • Lock management requires the Microsoft.Authorization/locks/write and Microsoft.Authorization/locks/delete permissions. Restrict these to a small admin group so that users who can deploy resources cannot also remove the protective lock. This provides separation of duties between deployers and lock managers.
  • For defense in depth, combine the CanNotDelete lock with Azure Policy. The lock prevents accidental deletion by authorized users, while Policy can enforce configuration compliance on resources deployed within the RG. Neither replaces the other; they serve complementary purposes.

questions.title: Identity: Group-Based Access
questions.scenario: You onboard 50 contractors for 3 months. They need Reader access to a subscription.

choices.text: Assign Reader role to each contractor individually
Use an Entra ID group assigned to Reader role at subscription scope
Create guest accounts without any role assignment

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: You have 50 users who need the same access for a fixed period. What is more maintainable: 50 individual assignments or a single assignment on a shared construct?

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Using an Entra ID group assigned to Reader at subscription scope (B) is operationally correct because it creates a single role assignment instead of 50 individual ones. Onboarding means adding a contractor to the group; offboarding means removing them. Option A (individual assignments) creates 50 role assignments to manage, 50 to revoke at contract end, and 50 entries cluttering the IAM access control list. Option C (Owner access) massively violates least privilege since Owner includes full RBAC management rights. Option D (no role assignment) means contractors cannot see anything, defeating the purpose. Group-based access is a fundamental Azure identity best practice that simplifies lifecycle management and audit reviews.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• For time-bound access, consider using Entra ID access reviews to automatically prompt group owners to review and confirm membership periodically. At the 3-month mark, an access review can automatically remove contractors who are no longer approved, preventing stale access.
  • If Entra ID P2 licensing is available, use Privileged Identity Management (PIM) for eligible group membership. Contractors activate their group membership when needed and it automatically deactivates after a configured duration, providing just-in-time access with full audit logging.
  • For B2B guest contractors, verify that Entra ID guest invite settings and cross-tenant access policies allow the guest accounts. Guest users are subject to additional Conditional Access policies and may have limited self-service capabilities compared to member users.
  • RBAC role assignments using groups create one assignment record on the subscription regardless of how many members the group has. This keeps the IAM blade clean and makes compliance audits simpler since reviewers only need to check one group assignment rather than 50 individual ones.

questions.title: Storage "Delete Protection" Mix-Up
questions.scenario: A team believes enabling blob soft delete meets a strict WORM compliance requirement.
questions.questionText: Is that correct? What do you use instead?

choices.text: Yes, soft delete is sufficient for WORM

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Soft delete and WORM serve fundamentally different purposes. Soft delete is a recoverability feature, while WORM requires a policy that actively prevents deletion.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: No, soft delete is not sufficient for WORM; you must use immutability policies (D). Soft delete is a recoverability feature that retains deleted blobs for a configurable period (1-365 days) so they can be undeleted, but it does not prevent the initial deletion. Anyone with delete permissions can still delete the blob, and after the soft delete retention period, the data is permanently gone. WORM (Write Once, Read Many) compliance requires that data cannot be deleted or modified at all during the retention period, which only immutability policies enforce. Option B (lifecycle management) automates deletion, which is the opposite of WORM. Option C (versioning plus soft delete) preserves versions but still does not prevent deletion of the blob or its versions.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Soft delete, versioning, and immutability are three distinct data protection features that complement but do not replace each other. Soft delete handles accidental deletion recovery. Versioning preserves previous blob states. Immutability enforces regulatory retention. A comprehensive strategy may use all three together.
  • Immutability policies support two modes: time-based retention (blobs cannot be deleted until a specific date) and legal hold (blobs cannot be deleted until the hold is explicitly removed). For WORM compliance, time-based retention with a locked policy is required because locked policies cannot be shortened or deleted.
  • A common misconception is that versioning with soft delete provides WORM-equivalent protection. It does not. An admin can still purge soft-deleted versions, and the soft delete retention period can be shortened. Only a locked immutability policy is irrevocable and therefore audit-proof for regulators.
  • When immutability and soft delete are both configured on a container, the interaction is: immutability prevents deletion during the retention period, and soft delete provides recovery if a blob is deleted after the immutability period expires. Plan the overlap between these retention windows based on your compliance and operational requirements.

questions.title: VM Access: Just Enough Exposure
questions.scenario: Security forbids direct public RDP/SSH to VMs. Admins still need remote access.

choices.text: Use Azure Bastion or a jump host pattern
Assign public IPs to all VMs
Use Azure DNS for VM access
Open NSG rules for RDP/SSH from any source

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: When direct public RDP/SSH is forbidden, you need a secure intermediary that provides remote access through a controlled, auditable entry point.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Azure Bastion or a jump host pattern (C) is the correct approach. Azure Bastion is a PaaS service that provides browser-based RDP/SSH access to VMs over TLS without exposing any public RDP/SSH ports. VMs need only private IPs, and admins connect through the Azure portal. A jump host (bastion VM in a hardened subnet) is the traditional alternative. Option A (open NSG from any source) directly violates the security requirement. Option B (public IPs on all VMs) creates unnecessary attack surface even if NSGs restrict access. Option D (Azure DNS) handles name resolution and has nothing to do with remote access security. Azure Bastion eliminates the need for public IPs on VMs while providing a fully auditable access path.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• Azure Bastion requires a dedicated subnet named AzureBastionSubnet with a minimum size of /26. It deploys into this subnet and uses a public IP for admin browser connections, but the RDP/SSH traffic to target VMs flows over the VNet private network. VMs themselves need no public IP or NSG rules allowing RDP/SSH from the internet.
  • Bastion supports two SKUs: Basic (single session, limited features) and Standard (multi-session, file upload/download, shareable links, IP-based connections). The Standard SKU also supports native client connections via the Azure CLI, enabling tools like PuTTY and mstsc instead of the browser-only experience.
  • All Bastion sessions are logged in the Activity Log, and session diagnostics can be sent to a Log Analytics workspace. This provides a full audit trail of who accessed which VM, when, and for how long, which is critical for compliance with security frameworks like SOC 2 and ISO 27001.
  • For hybrid scenarios where admins also need to access on-premises servers, combine Azure Bastion with VPN Gateway or ExpressRoute. Admins connect to Bastion in the portal, access a jump host in Azure, and then pivot to on-premises resources through the hybrid connection, keeping all access paths within controlled channels.

questions.title: End-to-End Scenario: Secure, Governed Landing Zone Slice
questions.scenario: You're asked to onboard a new application into Azure with: (1) enforced tags, (2) no public endpoints for storage, (3) least-privilege admin, (4) centralized logging, (5) budget alerts.

choices.text: Use default settings without any additional configuration
Rely on Azure Advisor recommendations only
Single subscription with all resources in one resource group
Management group policy + private endpoint + RBAC groups + Log Analytics + budgets

hints.label: Brief Hint
hints.content: Each of the five requirements maps to a specific Azure service, and the correct answer combines all five into a cohesive landing zone architecture.

hints.label: Complete Explanation
hints.content: Management group policy plus private endpoint plus RBAC groups plus Log Analytics plus budgets (D) is correct because it addresses all five requirements systematically. Enforced tags: Azure Policy initiative at the management group level with deny effect requiring CostCenter, Owner, and Env tags. No public endpoints: Private Endpoints for all storage services with private DNS zones, and public network access disabled. Least-privilege admin: Entra ID security groups with targeted RBAC roles at the resource group scope, not subscription-wide Contributor. Centralized logging: diagnostic settings on all resources routing to a shared Log Analytics workspace, with Azure Monitor alerts. Budget alerts: Azure Budgets with 50%, 80%, and 100% thresholds notifying the application team and finance. Options A, B, and C are fundamentally incomplete and do not meet any of the stated requirements.

hints.label: Deep Knowledge
hints.content:
• The three biggest operational traps in this architecture are: DNS configuration for Private Endpoints (if the privatelink DNS zones are not linked to all consuming VNets, clients resolve public IPs and connectivity fails silently), policy denials breaking deployments (teams get cryptic "deployment failed" errors when their resources violate tag or configuration policies), and workspace permissions being separate from resource RBAC (the app team can see their VMs but cannot query logs without explicit Log Analytics workspace access).
  • Separate resource groups for network resources (VNet, Private Endpoints, NSGs) and application resources (VMs, storage, App Service) provide cleaner RBAC boundaries. The network team manages the network RG; the app team manages the app RG. This prevents the app team from accidentally modifying network configurations while keeping their deployment autonomy.
  • For centralized logging, use Azure Policy with deployIfNotExists effect to automatically create diagnostic settings on new resources. Without this automation, every new storage account or VM deployed without diagnostic settings creates a monitoring blind spot. Combine with Azure Monitor alert rules for key failure scenarios (backup failure, high error rate, resource health degradation).
  • Landing zone design should be treated as a template that can be stamped out for new applications. Use infrastructure-as-code (Bicep, Terraform) to define the entire landing zone (subscription, RGs, policies, RBAC, networking, monitoring, budgets) as a repeatable module. This ensures consistency and reduces the onboarding time for each new application from weeks to hours.

term-rbac.name: Azure RBAC
term-rbac.definition: Authorization system for Azure resource actions using roles assigned at scopes.
term-rbac.examNote: Controls what actions identities can perform on Azure resources.

term-management-group.name: Management Group
term-management-group.definition: Hierarchy layer above subscriptions for consistent policy/RBAC inheritance.
term-management-group.examNote: Use for organizing subscriptions and applying consistent controls.

term-azure-policy.name: Azure Policy
term-azure-policy.definition: Governance engine that audits/enforces resource configuration using policy definitions/initiatives.
term-azure-policy.examNote: Use deny effect to block noncompliant deployments, audit to report only.

term-nsg.name: Network Security Group (NSG)
term-nsg.definition: Layer 3/4 ACL applied at subnet/NIC for traffic filtering.
term-nsg.examNote: Priority ordering matters - first match wins.

term-private-endpoint.name: Private Endpoint
term-private-endpoint.definition: Private IP interface in a VNet that maps to a PaaS resource; enables private access path.
term-private-endpoint.examNote: Requires correct DNS configuration to function properly.

term-managed-identity.name: Managed Identity
term-managed-identity.definition: Azure-managed identity for workloads; avoids storing credentials.

term-key-vault.name: Key Vault
term-key-vault.definition: Service for secrets/keys/certificates; commonly used with managed identity.
term-key-vault.examNote: Network restrictions can block access; ensure private endpoint/DNS if locked down.

term-log-analytics.name: Log Analytics Workspace
term-log-analytics.definition: Central store for logs queried via KQL.
term-log-analytics.examNote: Requires separate access permissions from resource RBAC.

term-availability-zone.name: Availability Zone
term-availability-zone.definition: Physically separate zone within a region; improves resilience against datacenter failures.
term-availability-zone.examNote: Zone support is regional; verify per region.

term-vmss.name: VM Scale Set (VMSS)
term-vmss.definition: Managed fleet of identical VMs supporting autoscale and uniform updates.
term-vmss.examNote: Best for stateless tiers; stateful workloads complicate scaling.
